answer_text:
Let

\[
g(x)=e^{-x}f(x).
\]

Since \(f(x)>0\), we have \(g(x)>0\). Also,

\[
g'(x)=e^{-x}f'(x)-e^{-x}f(x)=e^{-x}\bigl(f'(x)-f(x)\bigr)>0
\]

for all \(x\). Hence \(g\) is strictly increasing.

In particular, for \(x>0\),

\[
g(x)>g(0)=f(0),
\]

so

\[
f(x)=e^xg(x)>f(0)e^x.
\]

Now if \(k<1\), then

\[
\frac{f(0)e^x}{e^{kx}}=f(0)e^{(1-k)x}\to \infty
\]

as \(x\to\infty\), because \(1-k>0\). Therefore, for every \(k<1\), there exists \(X\) such that

\[
f(x)>e^{kx}
\]

for all \(x\ge X\).

The exponent \(1\) is sharp. For example, take

\[
g(x)=\frac{1}{1+e^{-x}},\qquad f(x)=e^xg(x).
\]

Then \(g'(x)>0\), so \(f'(x)>f(x)\), but \(g(x)<1\) for all \(x\), giving

\[
f(x)<e^x
\]

for all \(x\). Thus \(k=1\) is not guaranteed, and neither is any \(k>1\).

So the guaranteed values are \(k<1\), and the sharp critical value is

\[
\boxed{1}.
\]
